brackets.note: Flat rate. The statute sets 3.5% of net income for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 (down from 4%). Tax Foundation agrees. Kentucky has no head of household status, those filers use the same flat rate.

standardDeduction.note: The DOR release gives one amount, $3,360 for 2026. Per Tax Foundation footnote (z) a joint return gets the same single amount, it is not doubled. Married couples who both have income usually file separately on a combined return and each claim $3,360, which this schema's mfj value does not capture. Head of household uses the single amount.

rules.note: The $40 credits are read from KRS 141.020(3). The family size credit is from PolicyEngine. Louisville's occupational tax is in Tax Foundation's table. Contribution flags checked on 2026-11-12 against PolicyEngine US 2.118.6 (oracle/flags.py), which moves this state's tax by the same amount as this engine for 401k, HSA, IRA and health premium contributions. FSA and commuter benefits are not PolicyEngine inputs and rest on the state starting from federal income. Not read in the state's own instructions. No employee payroll contribution: the US Department of Labor's comparison lists worker unemployment contributions only in Alaska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania and disability insurance only in California, Hawaii, New Jersey, New York and Rhode Island, and no paid leave or similar program with an employee contribution was found for this state on 2026-11-12.
notes: Many Kentucky cities and counties levy occupational license taxes on wages. Not modeled.
Kentucky has no personal or dependent exemption. The only personal credits left are $40 each for age 65 or over and for blindness, and $20 for National Guard members.

Not modeled: the family size tax credit, a low-income credit that removes all tax when modified gross income is at or below the poverty threshold for the family size and phases out to nothing at about 133% of it.
Not modeled: married couples filing separately on a combined return each get the standard deduction, so a two-earner couple effectively deducts twice the amount shown for mfj.
